_meta.note: A 21-day countdown to the five principal Diwali observances. Days 1-16 are preparation and reflection; Days 17-21 are Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi (Choti Diwali), Lakshmi Puja (main Diwali), Govardhan Puja/Annakut, and Bhai Dooj. The main Diwali lamp (Day 19) sits at the mandala centre. Names and customs vary by region and community.
_meta.storyCard: Every lamp opens one mobile-first story card. Optional diya.story is the short episode narration; description remains the expandable cultural note. Video files stay lazy-loaded from the mp4 payload path.

_lampScaleNote: Global size multiplier applied to every diya's pos.w/pos.h at load time (see hydrateDiyas() in sketch.js). 1 = default size, 1.15 = 15% bigger, 0.9 = 10% smaller. Each lamp keeps its own centre point, so scaling grows/shrinks it in place instead of shifting it. To resize just ONE lamp, edit that diya's own pos.w/pos.h below instead — lampScale multiplies on top of those.

radialLayout._note: 21-day prototype: two 8-lamp rings, one 4-lamp festival ring, and main Diwali at the centre. All radii are fractions of canvas width.

scrollBanner._note: The 'Countdown to Diwali' title banner. Edit 'text' to change what it says, or call scrollBanner.setText('...') from the browser console.

diyas.description: Rangoli are beautiful geometric patterns drawn at home entrances using coloured powders, flower petals, and rice. They welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity, into the home.
Two weeks before Diwali, families deep-clean every corner of the home. A spotless house invites Goddess Lakshmi — she is said to visit only homes that are pure and welcoming.
As Dhanteras approaches, families may plan an auspicious purchase such as a utensil, gold, or silver. The observance itself is still ahead on Day 17, when it opens the five-day Diwali festival.
Mithai — traditional Indian sweets — are central to Diwali. Kaju Katli (cashew fudge), Gulab Jamun, Ladoo, and Barfi are gifted between families to share in the joy of the festival.
Diwali is a time to wear new clothes. Women wear vibrant sarees and lehengas in jewel tones — deep reds, royal blues, and golds — while men don kurta-pajamas or sherwanis.
A diya is a small clay oil lamp. Ghee or sesame oil fuels the cotton wick. Rows of diyas on windowsills and doorsteps symbolise the victory of light over darkness, and knowledge over ignorance.
Firecrackers have been part of Diwali for centuries — their lights and sounds are believed to ward off evil spirits. Today, many celebrate with sparklers and low-smoke alternatives.
Marigolds — called Genda Phool — are the flower of Diwali. Their vibrant orange and yellow hues symbolise auspiciousness and the sun. Garlands adorn doorways, idols, and offering plates.
The dhol drum and tabla drive the rhythms of Diwali celebrations. Classical Bharatanatyam and folk Garba and Dandiya dances fill community gatherings with energy and colour.
Diwali is celebrated by over a billion people globally — in India, UK, USA, Canada, Singapore, Fiji, South Africa, and beyond. It is a public holiday in over a dozen countries.

As Diwali approaches, many families make time for generosity: checking in with neighbours, sharing food, or supporting a local cause. The exact customs differ, but the spirit of care is widely shared.
Diwali carries different stories across regions and communities. This is a moment to ask family members which stories, memories, or values make the festival meaningful to them.
Prepare a welcoming corner at home: tidy a shared space, add colour, or make room for people you care about. Keep the ritual personal and suited to your household.
Plan a sweet to make, buy, or share. Mithai traditions are wonderfully varied, so choose something that connects you to your family, friends, or local community.
Choose one way to celebrate thoughtfully: reusable decor, lower-smoke lighting choices, a quieter gathering, or simply taking time to enjoy the lights together.
On the eve of the five Diwali days, pause and set an intention for the season: gratitude, renewal, connection, or a fresh beginning.

The first of the five principal Diwali days. Many households honour Dhanvantari and Lakshmi, light diyas, and make auspicious purchases of utensils, gold, or silver. Customs and deities emphasised vary by region and family.

The second day, also called Choti Diwali in many North Indian traditions. In several regions it recalls Krishna's victory over Narakasura; oil baths, cleansing rituals, and diyas are common, with customs varying across communities.

The central Diwali observance and the new-moon night. Many households perform Lakshmi Puja, light rows of diyas, share food, and gather with family. The stories and rituals associated with this night differ by region, faith, and household.

Often observed as Govardhan Puja or Annakut, recalling Krishna sheltering villagers beneath Govardhan Hill and giving thanks for nature's abundance. In some regions this date is instead marked as Bali Pratipada or Padwa.

The fifth and concluding day celebrates the bond between siblings. Many families observe a tilak and exchange blessings or gifts; it is also known as Bhai Phonta, Bhau Beej, or Yama Dwitiya in different regions.
